anchor: out of the battle I escaped
title: Title, date and publication
short: Probably drafted at Scarborough or Ripon in early 1918; unpublished in Owen's lifetime, first printed in Edith Sitwell's Wheels (1919) and in Poems (1920).
body: The poem belongs to the first half of 1918, probably written at Scarborough or Ripon (the Wilfred Owen Association says spring or early summer 1918; the dating is approximate). Owen was killed on 4 November 1918, a week before the Armistice. The poem appeared in the Sitwells' anthology Wheels (1919) and then in Poems (1920), edited by Sassoon, who had worked on the selection with Edith Sitwell; Sassoon's Introduction names it as the finest example of Owen's experiments in assonance and dissonance. Dennis Welland identified the title's source in Shelley's The Revolt of Islam, Canto V, where enemy soldiers seem 'like some brothers on a journey wide / Gone forth, whom now strange meeting did befall / In a strange land'. In summer 1918 Owen's draft contents list for his planned volume described the poem's 'motive' as 'Foolishness of War', according to Kerr.

title: Down some profound dull tunnel
short: The speaker descends into an underworld modelled on trench dug-outs and on literary hells (Dante, Keats's Fall of Hyperion).
body: The descent recalls the epic journey to the underworld (Odysseus in Odyssey 11, Aeneas in Aeneid 6, Dante in the Inferno, which Owen owned in Cary's translation). Muir thinks the general influence of the Inferno, a landscape of hell where the newly dead converse, matters more than any verbal echoes. John Middleton Murry, reviewing the poem in 1919, stressed its debt to Keats's Hyperion poems; and the Wilfred Owen Association suggests Sassoon's 'The Rear-Guard', about a soldier groping through an underground tunnel among the dead, as a probable prompt. The deep dug-outs and mine tunnels of the Western Front give the setting its literal basis. 'Profound' keeps its Latin sense of 'deep' (profundus).

sources.cite: Dante Alighieri, The Vision of Hell (Inferno), tr. H. F. Cary, Project Gutenberg

title: Titanic wars
short: The ancient war of the Titans against the Olympian gods, imagined as having carved the rock of this underworld.
body: In Greek myth the Titanomachy was the ten-year war in which Zeus and the Olympians overthrew the Titans, who were then imprisoned in Tartarus, deep beneath the earth (Hesiod, Theogony 617-735). Owen's tunnel runs through granite hollowed by those primeval conflicts, setting modern war in a mythic, geological perspective of endless violence; Keats's Hyperion, which Owen loved, describes the fallen Titans in their cavernous den. The phrase was one Yeats singled out as a cliche when dismissing Owen, according to Kerr, and opinions on its effectiveness remain divided.

title: groined
short: Hollowed into vaults: a 'groin' is the curved edge where two vaults intersect, as in a church crypt.
body: In architecture a groin is the edge formed by the intersection of two vaults, and to groin is to build with such vaults (OED). The granite tunnel is thus imagined as a natural crypt, appropriate to a place of the dead, and the word also carries a faint bodily suggestion. 'Groined' is the first half of the poem's first pararhyme pair with 'groaned' in the next line: the same consonant frame with a changed vowel (see 'Pararhyme'). Muir lists 'grained/groined' and 'escaped/scooped' as examples of Owen's strict practice, in which both the opening and closing consonants are matched.

title: Pararhyme
short: Couplets whose words share consonants but differ in their stressed vowels (escaped/scooped, groined/groaned): Owen's signature device, here used throughout.
body: The poem is written in pentameter couplets, but each pair is linked by pararhyme (also called consonant or half-rhyme): hall/Hell in Stallworthy's text, groined/groaned, mourn/moan, years/yours, killed/cold. The vowel usually falls in pitch from the first word to the second, producing an effect of dissonance and failed harmony suited to a dream of the dead. Sassoon's Introduction to Poems (1920) singled the poem out as the finest example of Owen's experiments in assonance and dissonance. Sources proposed include the French poet Jules Romains (suggested by Welland via Laurent Tailhade), Owen's early reading in J. A. Symonds on Shelley (Stallworthy), and, as Muir argued, a passage in Marlowe's Jew of Malta; Kerr is sceptical of Muir's Marlowe theory. John Middleton Murry's 1919 review first analysed the device's effect.

title: encumbered sleepers
short: The dead (or dying) lie in the tunnel like exhausted soldiers asleep in a dug-out, too weighed down to be roused.
body: 'Encumbered' means burdened or hampered, perhaps by full kit, perhaps by wounds or by death itself. The ambiguity of 'Too fast in thought or death' keeps the sleepers on the line between life and death; 'fast' means firmly held, as in 'fast asleep'. The image draws on real dug-outs crammed with sleeping or wounded men, and on epic underworlds full of shades. 'Bestirred', an archaism, keeps the slightly antique, visionary diction that Owen uses throughout.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

title: piteous recognition in fixed eyes
short: The dead man knows his killer; his staring eyes and lifted hands hover between blessing and accusation.
body: The 'fixed eyes' are those of a dead man, but they also recall the uncanny gazes of literary visions: 'Piteous' introduces the poem's key word pity (see 'The pity of war'). The gesture 'Lifting distressful hands as if to bless' is ambiguous: a plea, a priestly blessing, or the hands-up of surrender. The recognition is completed only in l. 39, when the stranger reveals that he is the enemy the speaker killed.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

title: And by his smile, I knew that sullen hall
short: The 1920 text's reading; Stallworthy's edition prints 'By his dead smile I knew we stood in Hell', making the underworld explicit.
body: The text shown here follows the first printed versions (Wheels 1919 and Poems 1920). Owen's manuscripts are untidy and unfinal, and the now-standard text in Stallworthy's critical edition reads 'With a thousand pains that vision's face was grained; / . . . By his dead smile I knew we stood in Hell', the version now most often printed; Muir quotes the 'sullen hall' and 'Hell' lines together as a pararhyme pair. 'Sullen hall' suggests a gloomy hall of the dead, perhaps recalling Valhalla or the halls of Hades, whereas 'Hell' names the place outright and pararhymes with 'hall'. Students should be aware that line wording varies between editions.

title: grained
short: Ingrained, deeply marked: the face is furrowed with fears, as wood is marked by its grain.
body: To be 'grained' is to have marks running through the substance, like the grain of wood or stone, or to be dyed deep (OED, 'ingrained'). The dead man's face carries the lines of a thousand fears, written into it rather than on its surface. The word belongs to the pararhyme pair groined/grained in Muir's list of Owen's 'sandwiching' rhymes, where initial and final consonants are both repeated. Stallworthy's text has 'pains' for 'fears'.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

title: the undone years
short: The years of life the dead man will never live: the loss of a future is the only cause for mourning in this place.
body: The speaker says there is no cause to mourn, since no shells reach this place; the dead man replies that there is one: 'the undone years'. 'Undone' means both not done (unlived) and ruined. The phrase introduces the lament for unfulfilled promise that dominates the middle section: the dead man's 'hope' was the same as the speaker's, suggesting from the start that the two are mirror images.

anchor: the wildest beauty in the world
title: hunting wild / After the wildest beauty
short: The dead man, like Owen, was a poet who pursued a beauty beyond conventional loveliness; Muir reads him as Owen's double.
body: The beauty sought is not that of 'eyes, or braided hair', the stock subjects of love poetry, but something that 'mocks the steady running of the hour', a Romantic ideal of beauty beyond time, reminiscent of Keats and Shelley, whom Owen idolised. Muir argues that the stranger is a German poet and 'Owen's doppelganger', speaking Owen's own words. Welland also read him as the poet's alter ego; Kerr notes that Dominic Hibberd later questioned the 'double' reading, and the poem itself does not settle it. Muir hears a native echo for the pararhymes 'wild/world' in Marlowe.

sources.cite: Dennis Welland, Wilfred Owen: A Critical Study (London: Chatto & Windus, 1960; rev. 1978), as reported by Muir

title: The pity of war
short: The 'truth untold' is the central idea of Owen's Preface: 'My subject is War, and the pity of War. The Poetry is in the pity.'
body: Owen's draft Preface to his intended collection, printed in Poems (1920), states that his subject is war and 'the pity of War', and that 'The Poetry is in the pity'; it adds that 'All a poet can do to-day is to warn'. The dead poet in the tunnel laments that his insight into that pity will now die untold. 'Distilled' suggests something extracted and concentrated, as in a still, like an essence or perhaps a poison, so war is both the occasion of pity and the process that refines it. Muir connects the passage directly with the Preface.

sources.cite: Wilfred Owen, Poems, ed. Siegfried Sassoon (London: Chatto & Windus, 1920), with Owen's Preface and Sassoon's Introduction, Project Gutenberg text

title: Now men will go content with what we spoiled
short: A prophecy that, without the warning the dead could have given, the survivors will either acquiesce or go on to new bloodshed.
body: With the truth 'untold', men will either be content with a spoiled world or, discontented, 'boil bloody, and be spilled', fight again and die. Muir calls this prophecy surprisingly little discussed and reads it as foreseeing post-war militarism and the dictatorships and wars of the next twenty years; Kerr finds the middle section's prophetic language largely incoherent, which he blames partly on the demands of pararhyme. The 'swiftness of the tigress' signals cruelty: Muir points out that in Owen's fragment 'Earth's wheels' (printed here as 'Another Version') it is better to 'break ranks' than trek from progress. Stallworthy compares David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1), which Muir thinks too eulogistic a parallel.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

title: Courage was mine . . . mastery
short: Balanced, chiastic lines in which the dead man claims the qualities of a poet; the draft version divides them between the two men.
body: The parallel syntax ('Courage was mine, and I had mystery; / Wisdom was mine, and I had mastery') is incantatory, and 'mystery/mastery' is an especially pure pararhyme. In the fragment printed as 'Another Version', the qualities are shared out ('Beauty is yours and you have mastery, / Wisdom is mine, and I have mystery'), which supports readings of the two speakers as complementary halves of one self. 'Mystery' may carry its older sense of a craft or trade, as well as of a hidden truth.

anchor: vain citadels that are not walled
title: vain citadels that are not walled
short: The world 'retreating' from progress marches into empty, undefended strongholds: false security and futile nationalist defences.
body: A citadel is a fortress commanding a city. These are 'vain' (empty, useless, and conceited) and 'not walled', offering no real protection, so the 'march' of the retreating world ends in illusion. The image ironically inverts the language of military advance. Stallworthy's text reads 'To miss the march of this retreating world / Into vain citadels that are not walled'; the 'Another Version' has 'old citadels'. Muir lists 'world/walled' among the pararhymes he links to Marlowe.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

title: much blood had clogged their chariot-wheels
short: Heroic and biblical war-chariots mired in blood; the dead poet would have washed them clean with deep truths.
body: The war-chariot is the emblem of ancient heroic warfare; in Iliad 20 the axle and rails of Akhilleus' chariot are spattered with blood thrown up by the wheels as he slaughters the Trojans. The Bible gives a parallel in the Egyptian chariots whose wheels the Lord took off in the Red Sea (Exodus 14:25). Owen imagines that, after the war, the poet would have gone up to cleanse the wheels with water 'from sweet wells', a prophetic and almost sacramental act of healing through truth. 'Truths that lie too deep for taint' echoes Wordsworth's 'Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears' (the last line of the Intimations Ode).

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 20.498-503 (tr. A. T. Murray), Perseus Digital Library

title: the cess of war
short: 'Cess' most likely means cesspool, the filth of war; older senses (a levy or tax) may also be heard.
body: The dead man would have poured out his spirit freely, but not through wounds and 'not on the cess of war'. 'Cess' is recorded as a short form of cesspool (OED), which fits the mud and sewage of the trenches; it also has the older sense of a tax or assessment, so the war becomes a levy paid in lives. The Irish phrase 'bad cess to . . .' (bad luck to) may add a curse-like undertone. The line contrasts a voluntary, Christ-like outpouring of the spirit with the meaningless spilling of blood.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

title: Foreheads of men have bled where no wounds were
short: Recalls Christ in Gethsemane, whose sweat fell 'as it were great drops of blood' (Luke 22:44): suffering of mind and spirit.
body: The image of bleeding without wounds alludes to Christ's agony in the Garden of Gethsemane, where his sweat became 'as it were great drops of blood' (Luke 22:44), and perhaps to the crown of thorns. The archive's 'Alternative line', 'Even as One who bled where no wounds were', makes the reference to Christ explicit with its capitalised 'One'. Owen often compared the infantryman with Christ, and the line implies inner suffering, the mental wounds of shell-shock and grief, which he had seen at Craiglockhart. Critics have read the line as the climax of the poem's prophetic, quasi-religious register, which Kerr traces in the poem's reception from Murry and Blunden onwards.

sources.cite: Jon Stallworthy, ed., Wilfred Owen: The Complete Poems and Fragments, 2 vols (London: Chatto & Windus / Hogarth / OUP, 1983), notes to the poem

anchor: I am the enemy you killed
title: I am the enemy you killed, my friend
short: The revelation: the stranger is the German soldier the speaker bayoneted. 'Enemy' and 'friend' are fused in one line.
body: The climactic line joins the opposites 'enemy' and 'friend' (the speaker's own greeting in l. 13: 'Strange, friend'). The stranger recognises the speaker by his frown as he 'jabbed and killed', implying bayonet fighting, and says he parried, but with hands 'loath and cold'. Readings divide: Welland and Muir see the enemy as the poet's double or alter ego, so that killing him is a kind of self-destruction; Hibberd, as Kerr reports, doubted this and preferred a more literal reading of two soldiers reconciled in death. Shelley's Revolt of Islam, the title's source, also depicts enemies reconciled as brothers.

title: Let us sleep now . . .
short: An ending in a broken half-line; scholars debate whether the poem is unfinished or deliberately ends as a fragment.
body: The poem stops on a short line of reconciliation and rest. Stallworthy asked whether Owen thought it finished. Muir argues it was meant to look like a fragment, on the model of Keats's Hyperion, which breaks off in mid-sentence; Kerr accepts that Owen probably saw the poem as incomplete, but suggests that the break may be deliberate and that the unfinished quality shows throughout its texture. The parenthesis that follows ('This poem was found among the author's papers. It ends on this strange note.') is an editorial note printed in Poems (1920), not Owen's text.

anchor: Earth's wheels run oiled with blood
title: Another Version
short: An earlier draft fragment, 'Earth's wheels', which Owen mined for 'Strange Meeting'; it shows the ideas in a different arrangement.
body: The archive's text adds a passage headed 'Another Version'. Stallworthy prints it as a separate fragment ('Earth's wheels run oiled with blood'), written between November 1917 and March 1918, and parts of it reappear in ll. 29-35 of the finished poem. In it the two figures resolve to break ranks and 'hold the open truth'; Muir uses it to show that the tigress stands for cruelty. Its image of men as pitchers sunk into deep wells and filled with truth develops the 'sweet wells' of the main poem, and its alternative last line points directly to Christ.
